paragraphs: The rain lashed against the stained-glass windows of Harrington Manor, each drop a tiny hammer against the funereal silence within. Detective Miles Corbin surveyed the scene, his gaze sweeping over the opulent library where Lord Alistair Harrington, a man whose wealth was matched only by his enemies, lay sprawled on an expensive Persian rug. A single, precise stab wound to the chest suggested a crime of passion, or perhaps cold, calculated revenge. His hand was clenched, not around a weapon, but around a small, ivory chess piece – a white knight.

Standing in the grand archway of the library was Lady Eleanor Harrington, a vision in silk and sorrow. Her face was a mask of aristocratic composure, yet a single, stray tear traced a path through her perfect makeup, a flaw in an otherwise flawless facade. "He was a difficult man, Detective," she said, her voice a low, steady whisper that seemed at odds with the tragedy. "He collected enemies like he collected rare books." Corbin noted the lack of hysterics, the chillingly pragmatic assessment of her late husband.

Corbin’s attention was drawn to a younger man pacing nervously in the adjacent drawing-room, his expensive suit rumpled and his tie loosened. This was Julian Croft, Lord Harrington's ambitious protégé and, until recently, his business partner. "We had a disagreement," Croft blurted out, his voice tight, before Corbin could even ask. "Alistair was planning to dissolve our partnership. He threatened to ruin me over the Kensington acquisition." He ran a hand through his hair, a gesture that failed to hide the tremor in his fingers.

A quiet presence materialized by the door, so silent that Corbin hadn't noticed his approach. It was Mr. Abernathy, the butler, a man who seemed as much a fixture of the manor as the ancient portraits on the walls. He was impeccably dressed, his face a roadmap of loyal service, but his eyes, dark and observant, missed nothing. "I found him, sir. Just after ten," Abernathy stated, his voice devoid of emotion. "Lord Harrington was in the middle of a game... he often played against himself to unwind." He gestured towards a small, ornate table where a chessboard sat, a solitary black king cornered on one side.

Corbin walked over to the chessboard, his eyes tracing the pieces on the mahogany and ivory squares. It was, as Abernathy had said, a game near its end, the black king trapped by a relentless white queen and rook. His gaze then drifted to the floor beneath the table, where a small glint of silver caught the lamplight. He stooped down, his gloved fingers plucking a cufflink from the deep-pile rug. It was intricately designed, a miniature black knight, its obsidian eye seeming to stare back at him accusingly.

Corbin held the cufflink up to the light, its polished surface reflecting the grim scene. He turned to the small, somber group. "Does this belong to anyone?" he asked, his voice even. Julian Croft's eyes widened almost imperceptibly, and his hand flew to his right shirt cuff. The cuff was bare, the small fabric hole a stark confirmation. "It... it must have come loose," he stammered, his earlier agitation escalating into visible panic. "We argued, yes, but I didn't... I would never..."

"An argument about a business deal that could ruin you," Corbin mused aloud, his eyes fixed on Croft. "You were here, you argued with the victim just before he died, and you leave a personal item at the scene of the crime." Each word was a carefully placed weight, pressing down on the young man's crumbling composure. Lady Eleanor watched the exchange with an unreadable expression, her hands clasped tightly in front of her, while Abernathy stood as still and silent as a statue.

A throat cleared softly from the doorway, drawing all eyes to a mousy-haired woman in a severe grey dress, clutching a leather-bound folio to her chest. "Forgive me, Detective," she said, her voice barely a whisper. "I am Beatrice Vance, Lord Harrington's personal assistant. I overheard the… disagreement. Lord Harrington told Mr. Croft their meeting was over at precisely nine-thirty. He was quite firm. He said he would not be blackmailed." The final word hung in the air, a damning accusation that made Julian Croft's face turn ashen.

Corbin turned his attention to Beatrice Vance. She seemed timid, almost frightened to be the center of attention, yet her gaze was steady. "Blackmailed? What was Mr. Croft holding over him?" he asked. Beatrice clutched her folio tighter. "I... I'm not certain of the specifics, Detective. But Mr. Croft had discovered some… discrepancies… in the initial funding for the Harrington empire. Old secrets, I believe. Lord Harrington was furious that he would dare to use them against him."

"Old secrets, indeed," Julian Croft scoffed, a flicker of defiance returning to his eyes. "Alistair built his fortune on a lie, a swindle that bankrupted his first partner, a man named Thomas Croft—my father. He thought I didn't know. I confronted him with the proof tonight. He didn't threaten to ruin me; he laughed. He told me I was just as powerless as my father had been." The confession, raw and bitter, painted a powerful motive: revenge for a generational wrong.

"So you admit to a heated confrontation over a deep, personal grievance mere moments before he was murdered," Corbin summarized, his tone hardening. He paced the length of the Persian rug, his footsteps unnervingly loud in the tense silence. "You had motive, you were here at the time of death, and you left evidence connecting you to the scene. It's not looking good for you, Mr. Croft." He stopped and turned, his shadow falling over the terrified young man. "Where is the murder weapon?"

"I don't know! I didn't kill him!" Croft's voice cracked, desperation creeping in. "After he dismissed me, I went to the smoking room to pour myself a drink, to figure out what my next move was. I was there for at least half an hour, maybe more, stewing in my own failure. Anyone could have gone into the library then. Lady Eleanor, Abernathy... even her," he added, with a desperate nod towards the seemingly meek Beatrice Vance.

Corbin’s gaze shifted to Lady Eleanor, who had remained a pillar of icy calm throughout the interrogation. “Mrs. Harrington, where were you after Mr. Croft’s… meeting concluded?” Her chin lifted slightly. “I was in the east wing conservatory, Detective. I find the night-blooming jasmine to be a great comfort when Alistair was in one of his moods. I was there until Abernathy brought me the dreadful news.” Her alibi was pristine, delivered without a hint of hesitation.

Next, Corbin addressed the butler. "Mr. Abernathy, you found the body. What were your movements this evening?" The old butler’s posture remained ramrod straight. "After serving his Lordship his customary glass of port at nine o'clock, I retired to the kitchens to oversee preparations for tomorrow. I did my rounds of the ground floor at ten, ensuring all was secure. It was then that I discovered..." He trailed off, his professional mask slipping for a fraction of a second to reveal a flicker of genuine distress before it was gone.

"And you, Miss Vance?" Corbin asked, turning to the personal assistant who still hovered by the door. "Where were you after you overheard the argument?" She flinched, as if surprised to be addressed again. "I was in my office, sir, in the west wing. There were ledgers to be finalized. I… I often work late. I heard nothing after Mr. Croft left the library. The house is so large, the walls so thick." Her alibi, like the others, was plausible, a neat parcel of time and place.

Corbin returned to the body, kneeling beside Lord Harrington. The ivory knight was still clutched in his stiffening fingers. A man who plays chess against himself, Corbin thought, a man obsessed with strategy and control. He gently pried the fingers open. As the chess piece came free, he noticed something else: a small, almost invisible smudge of dark ink on the victim’s thumb, the kind one gets from handling freshly printed documents or, perhaps, a leaky fountain pen.

His eyes scanned the room again, looking for a source. Lord Harrington’s ornate desk was a model of tidiness, not a document in sight. There was an antique letter opener, a silver-framed photograph of his wife, and a gold-plated fountain pen resting in its holder, its nib clean. Nothing seemed out of place, nothing to suggest a struggle or any last-minute paperwork. The ink smudge was a loose thread, a detail without context, yet it snagged at the detective's mind.

"Mr. Croft," Corbin said, turning back to the primary suspect. "You said you confronted him with proof. What form did this proof take?" Julian hesitated, then sighed in resignation. "It was a set of photocopied ledgers and a letter from my father, detailing Alistair's betrayal. I had them in a briefcase. When he laughed at me, I... I threw the briefcase on his desk in disgust. I left it there." Corbin walked to the desk, running his gloved hand over the polished mahogany surface. There was no briefcase.

"The briefcase is gone," Corbin stated flatly, his gaze sweeping over the faces of the other three. "Someone took it." He looked at Lady Eleanor, whose expression remained impassive. He looked at Abernathy, whose posture was as unyielding as ever. Then he looked at Beatrice Vance, who was now clutching her own leather folio so tightly her knuckles were white. The folio suddenly seemed less a symbol of her profession and more like a shield.

Corbin walked slowly towards Beatrice, his footsteps echoing on the parquet floor. "Miss Vance, you said you were in your office all evening. Finalizing ledgers." His voice was soft, almost conversational. "It is curious, then, that Lord Harrington, a man known for his meticulous nature, would have an ink stain on his thumb when there is no ink to be seen on his desk. Unless, of course, he was handling documents just before he died. Documents that are no longer here."

Beatrice Vance began to tremble, her mousy demeanor dissolving into one of pure terror. "I... I don't know what you mean," she stammered, taking an involuntary step backward. Corbin's eyes dropped to the folio she was still hugging to her chest. "Let me see what you have there, Miss Vance," he said, his voice no longer gentle. It was a command, sharp and absolute, cutting through the tense air of the library.

With shaking hands, Beatrice held out the folio. Corbin took it and unfastened the clasp. Inside were not company ledgers, but the very documents Julian Croft had described, along with another set of papers: a freshly signed last will and testament. Lord Harrington's signature was still slightly damp at the bottom, and a single, smeared thumbprint marred the corner of the page. The new will disinherited his wife, dissolved his partnership with Croft, and left the entirety of the Harrington fortune and empire to one person: Beatrice Vance.

"He was going to leave it all to me," Beatrice whispered, the words tumbling out in a frantic rush. "He said he saw in me a loyalty and intelligence he'd never found in anyone else. Julian's blackmail attempt was the last straw. He called me into the library after Julian left, to sign the new will. He wanted a witness to his triumph over his so-called 'betters'." Her eyes darted wildly between the stunned faces of Lady Eleanor and Julian Croft.

"He signed it," she continued, her voice rising with a frantic edge, "and then... he laughed. He laughed the same way he laughed at Julian. He said the will was his final, perfect move. He told me I would be his puppet, that I would run his empire from beyond the grave, forever indebted and under his control, just like everyone else. He wasn't giving me a gift; he was forging a new chain." Her hand drifted to the letter opener on the desk, the one Corbin had dismissed as a simple desk accessory. "I was just another piece on his board. He thought he had me in checkmate. But even a pawn," she said, a chilling calm descending over her, "can take a king."

Corbin looked from the letter opener to the wound on Harrington's chest, then back to the quiet, mousy woman who had confessed to murder. The chess game on the table finally made sense. It wasn't about a black king cornered by a white queen; it was about the overlooked piece, the one nobody pays attention to until it reaches the other side of the board and gains unimaginable power. The cufflink, the argument, the financial ruin—it was all a brilliant misdirection, a sideshow orchestrated by Harrington's own arrogance. The true motive wasn't revenge for the past; it was a desperate, bloody bid for a future that was about to be stolen.

first_paras: In the adjacent drawing-room, the household was assembled like a collection of porcelain figures, fragile and cold. Lady Eleanor Harrington, the victim’s much younger wife, dabbed at her eyes with a lace handkerchief, her sobs too perfect, too rhythmic. Standing by the mantelpiece was Julian Croft, Lord Harrington’s nephew and heir apparent, his jaw set, his gaze fixed on the storm outside. He adjusted his cufflinks, a sliver of ivory peeking from his sleeve, a detail that Corbin filed away. The butler, Abernathy, stood sentinel by the door, his face a mask of practiced stoicism.

Huddled by the grand fireplace, a stark contrast to the room's chill, were the four key players in this unfolding drama. Eleanor Harrington, the victim's young and icily composed widow, stood with a posture so perfect it seemed rehearsed. Her eyes, dry and assessing, followed Corbin's every move. Beside her, Julian Croft, Lord Harrington's nephew and heir apparent, nervously wrung his hands, his face a mask of poorly concealed agitation. Beatrice Vance, a distant cousin and long-term guest at the manor, wept softly into a silk handkerchief, while Abernathy, the family's ramrod-straight butler, stood sentinel by the door, his face ashen but unreadable.

Huddled by the grand fireplace, a collection of pale faces stared back at him, each a potential player in this grim drama. Lord Harrington’s young wife, Eleanor, stood rigid, her expression a mask of porcelain grief. Beside her, Julian Croft, the victim’s nephew and a struggling artist, paced like a caged tiger, his hands clenched and his jaw tight. It was common knowledge that he and his uncle had argued violently just that afternoon over his inheritance. Seated calmly in a wingback chair was Beatrice Vance, a shrewd business rival who stood to gain immensely from Harrington’s demise. And then there was Abernathy, the family butler for over three decades, standing silently by the doorway, a ghost in his own home, his face betraying nothing but a deep, weary sorrow.

Huddled by the grand fireplace, a tableau of forced solemnity, were the four individuals who had been in the manor at the time of death. Lady Eleanor Harrington, the victim's wife, stood apart, her grief a mask of icy composure that failed to conceal the flicker of something colder in her eyes. Across from her, Julian Croft, Harrington's ambitious business partner, paced restlessly, his gaze darting not to the body, but to the mahogany desk laden with contracts and financial reports. Beatrice Vance, Lord Harrington's young and spirited niece, was curled in a wingback chair, her quiet sobs the only sound to challenge the drumming of the rain. And by the doorway, a silent sentinel, was Abernathy, the butler, his face an unreadable map of decades of service.

Corbin’s eyes lifted from the body to the four figures huddled near the grand fireplace, their faces a gallery of shock and carefully constructed grief. There was Eleanor Harrington, the victim’s young wife, her posture unnervingly perfect, her beauty as cold and sharp as a shard of ice. Next to her, Julian Croft, Lord Harrington's business partner, vibrated with a barely contained fury, his knuckles white as he clenched and unclenched his fists. Beatrice Vance, the mousy niece who also served as Alistair’s personal secretary, was a crumpled heap of quiet sobs. And in the background, almost melting into the mahogany-paneled walls, stood Abernathy, the butler, a stoic ghost who had served the family for decades.

Corbin noted the lack of hysterics, the chillingly pragmatic assessment of her late husband.

Abernathy, the family butler for over four decades, stood by the mantelpiece, a man who seemed as much a part of the manor's architecture as the ancient grandfather clock that ticked solemnly in the hall. His face, a roadmap of dignified service, was impassive. "I was bringing his lordship his nightly brandy when I discovered him," he stated, his voice a low, gravelly monotone that betrayed no emotion. Corbin noticed the butler's hands were perfectly steady, his gaze unwavering as it rested on the body of the man he had served for most of his life.

From the shadows of the hall, the butler, Abernathy, emerged. He was a man who seemed to have been born old, his face a roadmap of loyal service and quiet disapproval. "It was I who discovered him, sir," he stated, his voice as dry as old parchment, betraying no emotion. "I came to inform him that his late-night tea was ready." His gaze, however, flickered not to the body, but to the grand mahogany desk. "The silver letter opener is gone from its stand. Lord Harrington was very particular about it."

The butler, a man who introduced himself simply as Abernathy, stood ramrod straight by the fireplace, his face as impassive as the marble mantelpiece behind him. Decades of service were etched into the lines around his eyes, yet they betrayed nothing. "It was I who discovered his lordship," he stated, his tone devoid of emotion. "I was bringing his ten o'clock brandy. The library door was ajar, which was unusual. His lordship always insisted on absolute privacy when he worked. I found him… as you see him now."

From the shadows of the hallway, a figure emerged, as silent and straight-backed as a marble statue. It was Abernathy, the family butler, his face a gaunt mask of practiced impassivity. "I served his Lordship his final glass of brandy at nine o'clock, Detective," he stated, his voice a dry rustle of old parchment. "He was... agitated. After Mr. Croft's departure. The shouting from the library was quite unseemly." His gaze flickered towards Julian Croft for just a moment, a subtle but undeniable accusation.

The butler, Abernathy, stood just outside the library doors, his posture as rigid as the suit of armor in the hallway. He had served the Harrington family for forty years, a silent witness to their triumphs and indiscretions. He cleared his throat, a dry, rustling sound. "The final argument between his Lordship and Mr. Croft was... particularly vicious, sir," he offered, his voice devoid of emotion. "I heard raised voices from the pantry. His Lordship mentioned something about 'utter betrayal' and 'a final checkmate.' It was most unbecoming."

A quiet presence materialized by the door, so silent that Corbin hadn't noticed his approach. It was Mr. Abernathy, the butler, a man who seemed as much a fixture of the manor as the ancient portraits on the walls. He gestured towards a small, ornate table where a chessboard sat, a solitary black king cornered on one side.

Corbin straightened up, the cufflink cold in his palm. He walked back towards the drawing-room where Julian Croft was still pacing, his expression unreadable. Without a word, he opened his hand. The color drained from Croft's face as he stared at the small, silver object. Corbin’s eyes flickered down to the young man’s wrist. The French cuff of his expensive shirt was bare on one side, the silk gaping open. “I… I suppose it is,” Croft stammered, his earlier agitation escalating into visible panic. “I must have lost it when I came in earlier.”

Corbin straightened up, the cufflink resting in his palm. He walked back into the drawing-room where Julian Croft was still pacing, his agitation having found no release. Without a word, Corbin held out his hand. Julian glanced down, his eyes widening in recognition before he quickly masked his expression, a flicker of panic crossing his face. "I've never seen that before in my life," he said, his voice a little too loud, a little too defensive. But Corbin's gaze had already fallen to Julian's left wrist, where a French cuff was fastened not with a matching link, but with a small, makeshift paperclip.

Corbin straightened up, the cufflink resting in his palm. He glanced back at Julian Croft, who had stopped his nervous pacing and was now watching the detective with wide, anxious eyes. As Croft's hand moved to adjust his collar, Corbin saw it – the glint of a matching silver cufflink on his right sleeve, its design unmistakable. The other cuff, however, was bare, a small, frayed thread marking the spot where its partner had been violently torn away. Croft saw the detective's gaze flicker from his wrist to the evidence in his hand, and a fresh wave of pallor washed over his face.

Corbin straightened up, holding the cufflink between his thumb and forefinger. He walked back towards the drawing-room, his eyes fixed on Julian Croft. "I believe this belongs to you, Mr. Croft," he said, his voice level as he held it out. Julian’s eyes widened as he glanced down at his own French cuffs. One was indeed bare. "It... it is," he stammered, a bead of sweat tracing a path down his temple. "But I don't know how it got in there. I haven't set foot in this room since this afternoon." The denial was too quick, too desperate. To Corbin, it sounded less like a statement of fact and more like a hastily constructed alibi.

The final person waiting to be questioned was Beatrice Vance, a renowned art historian and a fierce competitor of Lord Harrington's in the cutthroat world of high-stakes auctions. She was sharp, dressed in a severe black suit that seemed to amplify her intensity. "Yes, Detective, we had a row," she admitted without hesitation, her arms crossed tightly. "Alistair poached a client and a priceless manuscript from me last week. I told him he was a ruthless monster who deserved whatever was coming to him. Prophetic, wouldn't you say?" Her candor was disarming, almost defiant.

Corbin held the cufflink up to the light, its polished surface reflecting the grim scene. He turned to the small, somber group. "Does this belong to anyone?" he asked, his voice even. Julian Croft's eyes widened almost imperceptibly, and his hand flew to his right shirt cuff. The cuff was bare, the small fabric hole a stark confirmation. "It... it must have come loose," he stammered, his earlier agitation escalating into visible panic. "We argued, yes, but I didn't... I would never..."

Suddenly, a new voice, sharp and cutting, sliced through the tension. "Don't be absurd, Detective. Julian may be a fool, but he's no killer." Beatrice Vance, Lord Harrington's sharp-tongued sister, strode into the room, her tweed suit and sensible shoes a stark contrast to Eleanor's grieving widow attire. She surveyed the scene with a gimlet eye, her gaze lingering for a moment on the body of her brother with something akin to distaste. "If you're looking for someone with a reason to want Alistair dead, you'll need a much longer list."

Suddenly, a fourth voice, sharp and cutting, sliced through the tense atmosphere. "Don't be a fool, Julian. Tell the man the truth." Beatrice Vance, Lord Harrington's sharp-tongued sister, strode into the library, her heels clicking decisively on the polished floorboards. She was a formidable woman in her late fifties, with a gaze that could wither a lesser man. "My brother was a tyrant. Julian is many things—ambitious, arrogant, occasionally foolish—but he is not a killer."

A sharp, commanding voice cut through the tension. "What is the meaning of this circus?" A woman strode into the library, her posture ramrod straight, her tweed suit immaculate despite the storm. Her grey eyes, sharp as shards of ice, swept over the scene, lingered on the body with a flicker of something unidentifiable, and then settled on Julian Croft with undisguised contempt. "Beatrice," Eleanor said, a hint of weariness in her tone. "My late husband's sister, Miss Beatrice Vance." Beatrice ignored her, her gaze still locked on the trembling protégé. "I always knew you were a spineless little viper, Croft. Did Alistair finally grow tired of your sycophantic posturing?"

A whirlwind of damp tweed and fury burst into the hall, shoving a uniformed officer aside as if he were a piece of furniture. This was Beatrice Vance, Lord Harrington’s younger sister, a woman who wore her emotions like armor. Her eyes, red-rimmed but blazing, landed on Julian Croft, who flinched under their intensity. "You!" she screeched, her voice cracking with a potent mix of grief and rage. "I warned Alistair about you! About your greed! You've finally done it, haven't you?"

A sharp, clear voice cut through the tension. "Julian was not the only one to argue with Lord Harrington tonight." A woman stepped forward from the shadows of the hallway, her high heels clicking softly on the polished floorboards. She was Beatrice Vance, Lord Harrington’s private secretary, her severe hairstyle and tailored suit giving her an air of professional efficiency that even grief couldn't entirely dismantle. "I heard them shouting from my office. But Alistair argued with everyone. It was his primary form of communication." Her eyes, cool and analytical, flicked from Croft to Corbin, assessing the situation with a detached curiosity.

A throat cleared softly from the doorway, drawing all eyes to a mousy-haired woman in a severe grey dress, clutching a leather-bound folio to her chest. "Forgive me, Detective," she said, her voice barely a whisper. "I am Beatrice Vance, Lord Harrington's personal assistant. I overheard the… disagreement. Lord Harrington told Mr. Croft their meeting was over at precisely nine-thirty. He was quite firm. He said he would not be blackmailed." The final word hung in the air, a damning accusation that made Julian Croft's face turn ashen.

Corbin's gaze snapped back to Julian Croft, who was now shaking his head vehemently. "Blackmail? That's insane! I found proof he'd cheated his original partners, the very men who helped him build this company! I was confronting him, demanding he make it right, not blackmailing him!" His defense, however noble it sounded, came out as a desperate, rambling plea. To Corbin, it sounded exactly like the panicked denial of a man caught in a lie, a man who had escalated from threats to murder when his demands were not met.

"So, it wasn't just a business disagreement," Corbin stated, his gaze snapping back to Julian Croft. "You tried to blackmail him, and he refused to be intimidated. It seems your options were running out, Mr. Croft." Julian paled, shaking his head frantically. "No, that's not how it was! I found some old letters, proof that he cheated his original partner—Eleanor's father—out of his share of the company decades ago. I was trying to convince him to do the right thing, to make restitution to his own wife!" His explanation sounded desperate, a flimsy attempt to reframe a sordid threat as a noble act.

Corbin’s gaze snapped back to Julian Croft, whose face was now slick with a sheen of cold sweat. "So it wasn't just a business disagreement, Mr. Croft. It was blackmail." Julian's denial was a frantic wave of his hands. "No! I wasn't blackmailing him! I was... I was confronting him. The discrepancies Miss Vance mentioned... they proved he swindled my father out of his original stake in the company decades ago. I just wanted what was rightfully mine!" His voice cracked, the confession of a motive hanging in the air, more damning than any lie he could have told.

Corbin’s focus snapped back to Julian Croft, the pieces of a motive falling neatly into place. "So, it wasn't just a business disagreement, Mr. Croft. It was blackmail," the detective stated, his voice flat and accusatory. "What were these old secrets you were using as leverage?" Julian shook his head wildly, his face slick with sweat. "No! It wasn't like that! He was making reckless decisions, burying the company... I only brought up the past to make him see reason, to protect my own investment!" The plea sounded hollow, the desperate excuse of a man cornered, while Beatrice Vance looked on, her face a mask of what could be mistaken for pity.

"So Croft had a motive for blackmail, and when that failed, it turned to murder," Corbin summarized, pacing slowly in front of Julian. "He threatened to expose old family secrets, and you killed him to shut him up. Or perhaps it was the other way around. He threatened to ruin you, and you snapped." Julian shook his head violently, sweat beading on his forehead. "No! That's not how it happened. He was the one who was unreasonable! He laughed in my face!"

"Old secrets, indeed," Julian Croft scoffed, a flicker of defiance returning to his eyes. "Alistair built his fortune on a lie, a swindle that bankrupted his first partner, a man named Thomas Croft—my father. He thought I didn't know. I confronted him with the proof tonight. He didn't threaten to ruin me; he laughed. He told me I was just as powerless as my father had been." The confession, raw and bitter, painted a powerful motive: revenge for a generational wrong.

"I don't know! I didn't have a weapon!" Croft insisted, his voice cracking. "After he laughed at me, I stormed out. I went to the gardens to cool off. I walked by the conservatory for... I don't know, twenty minutes, half an hour? I was furious. When I came back inside, Abernathy was on the telephone, calling the police." His story, while plausible, was conveniently devoid of witnesses. It was his word against a mountain of circumstantial evidence.

"I don't know! I didn't have a weapon!" Croft insisted, his voice cracking. "After he laughed at me, I stormed out. I went to the gardens to cool off. Abernathy saw me leave through the terrace doors. Tell him!" he pleaded, turning a desperate gaze towards the butler. Abernathy gave a slow, deliberate nod. "That is correct, sir. I saw Mr. Croft exit to the terrace at approximately nine forty-five. He seemed… agitated." The confirmation offered an alibi, but a flimsy one. The gardens were large, but not so large one couldn't slip back inside unnoticed.

"I don't know! I left after he dismissed me," Julian insisted, his voice cracking. "I went straight to the guest quarters to pack my things. I was leaving tonight, for good." He looked around desperately, his gaze falling on Lady Eleanor. "Eleanor, please, you know I couldn't do something like this. Tell him." Lady Eleanor, however, remained impassive, her expression a cool, distant mask of grief. "I was in my chambers, Julian," she stated flatly. "I heard nothing after your shouting match concluded."

Julian Croft shook his head frantically, his hands raised in a gesture of surrender. "I don't know! I left the library immediately after he dismissed me. I went to the drawing-room to pour myself a drink, to figure out my next move. Abernathy saw me. Tell him!" he pleaded, turning a desperate gaze towards the butler. Abernathy gave a slow, deliberate nod. "Indeed, sir. Mr. Croft entered the drawing-room at approximately nine-thirty-five. He appeared… distressed. He remained there until I discovered the body."

"I don't know! I didn't have a weapon!" Croft insisted, his voice cracking. "I left the library after he dismissed me. I went to the drawing-room to pour myself a drink, to figure out what to do next. Abernathy saw me leave. Tell him!" He looked desperately towards the butler, pleading for corroboration. Abernathy gave a slow, deliberate nod. "That is correct, sir. Mr. Croft exited the library at approximately nine-forty. I was in the hall, polishing silver."
